accumulators-and-counters.label: Accumulators and Counters
accumulators-and-counters.summary: Initialize state before a loop, update a counter or accumulator during the loop, and use the final stored result after all relevant items have been processed.

sketch1.title: Counting only when a condition is true

ex1.title: Identify the accumulator
ex1.prompt:
In this code, which variable is the accumulator?

```python
numbers = [2, 4, 6]
total = 0
for n in numbers:
    total = total + n
print(total)
```
ex1.hint: Look for the variable that keeps the running sum.

help.concept: An accumulator stores a result that is repeatedly updated across loop iterations.
help.hint_2: `total` keeps the sum built so far.

ex2.title: Choose the best starting value
ex2.prompt: You want to count how many letters in a word are vowels. What is the best starting value for the counter variable?
ex2.hint: Before the loop runs, zero matches have been found.

help.concept: A counter starts at zero when it represents how many matches have occurred so far.
help.hint_1: No characters have been checked before the loop starts.

ex3.title: Pick the counter patterns
ex3.prompt: Which code lines are valid ways to increase a counter by 1? Choose all correct answers.
ex3.hint: The new counter value must be the old counter value plus one.

help.concept: `count = count + 1` and `count += 1` both increment the stored counter by one.
help.hint_2: Subtracting one moves in the opposite direction.

ex4.title: Recognize accumulator behavior
ex4.prompt: Which statements correctly describe accumulators? Choose all that apply.
ex4.hint: An accumulator preserves and updates a running result across iterations.

help.concept: Accumulators can store different kinds of running results as long as each update builds from the current stored value.
help.hint_2: A text accumulator can start at `""` and grow by concatenation.

options.a: A numeric accumulator can start at `0`.
options.b: An accumulator is usually updated inside the loop.
options.c: An accumulator must be reset to its starting value every iteration.
options.d: A string accumulator can build text step by step.

ex5.title: Order the counting steps
ex5.prompt: Arrange these steps to count how many vowels are in a word.
ex5.hint: Initialize first; the increment belongs after the condition matches.

help.concept: Conditional counting follows initialize → iterate → test → increment.
help.hint_1: The counter must exist before the loop begins.
help.hint_2: Increase it only after the current item passes the test.

tokens.t2: Loop through each character in the word
tokens.t3: Check whether the character is a vowel

ex6.title: Order the running total logic
ex6.prompt: Arrange these code ideas in the correct order for summing numbers in a list.
ex6.hint: Initialize before the loop and print only after all updates are complete.

help.concept: A running total follows initialize → iterate → update → use the final value.
help.hint_1: The accumulator update belongs inside the loop.
help.hint_2: The final print belongs after the loop.

ex7.title: Fill the counter start value
ex7.prompt: Complete the code so the counter starts correctly.
ex7.hint: Before any matches are counted, the stored count is zero.

help.concept: Counters represent how many matching events have occurred so far.
help.hint_1: At the start, none have occurred.

ex8.title: Fill the accumulator variable
ex8.prompt: Complete the line so it adds the current number to the running total.
ex8.hint: The same variable appears on both sides because it stores the running sum.

help.concept: An accumulator update reads the old accumulated value and stores the new one back under the same name.
help.hint_2: The left side should also be `total`.

ex9.title: Build a running numeric total
ex9.prompt: Read one line of space-separated integers. Use a `for` loop and a numeric accumulator named `total` to add every value, then print the final total.
ex9.hint: Start `total` at 0, convert each part to an integer, and add it into the running total.

help.concept: A numeric accumulator keeps the sum built from all values processed so far.
help.hint_2: Inside the loop, update with `total = total + int(part)` or the equivalent `+=` form.

ex9.starterCode:
parts = input().split()
total = 0
# Add every number into total
print(total)
ex9.solutionCode:
parts = input().split()
total = 0
for part in parts:
    total = total + int(part)
print(total)

0.message: Initialize `total` before the loop and update it from its previous value inside the loop.

ex10.title: Count matching characters
ex10.prompt: Read one word. Count how many lowercase vowels (`a`, `e`, `i`, `o`, `u`) it contains and print the final count.
ex10.hint: Start the counter at 0 and increase it only when the current character is a vowel.

help.concept: A conditional counter changes by one only when the current item matches the condition.
help.hint_1: Loop through `word` one character at a time.

ex10.starterCode:
word = input()
vowel_count = 0
# Count lowercase vowels
print(vowel_count)

0.message: Initialize `vowel_count` before the loop and increment it only inside the vowel condition.

ex11.title: Accumulate only matching numbers
ex11.prompt: Read one line of space-separated integers. Add only the even values to `even_total`, then print the final total.
ex11.hint: Convert each part, test whether it is even, and update the accumulator only for matches.

help.concept: A conditional accumulator skips values that fail the condition and adds only matching values.

ex11.starterCode:
parts = input().split()
even_total = 0
# Add only even numbers into even_total
print(even_total)
ex11.solutionCode:
parts = input().split()
even_total = 0
for part in parts:
    n = int(part)
    if n % 2 == 0:
        even_total = even_total + n
print(even_total)

0.message: Initialize `even_total` before the loop and update it only when the converted number is even.

ex12.title: Count positive numbers
ex12.prompt: Read one line of space-separated integers. Count how many values are greater than 0 and print the final count.
ex12.hint: Start `count` at 0 and increment only when the converted number is positive.

help.concept: This is the numeric version of a conditional counter.

ex12.starterCode:
parts = input().split()
count = 0
# Count values greater than zero
print(count)
ex12.solutionCode:
parts = input().split()
count = 0
for part in parts:
    n = int(part)
    if n > 0:
        count = count + 1
print(count)

0.message: Initialize `count` before the loop and increment it only when `n > 0`.

ex13.title: Build a text accumulator
ex13.prompt: Read one word. Build a string named `result` by adding each character followed by `-`, then print the completed result.
ex13.hint: Start with an empty string and update `result` inside the loop.

help.concept: A string accumulator follows the same initialize-and-update pattern as a numeric accumulator.
help.hint_2: Inside the loop, use `result = result + ch + "-"`.

ex13.starterCode:
word = input()
result = ""
# Add each character and a dash to result
print(result)
ex13.solutionCode:
word = input()
result = ""
for ch in word:
    result = result + ch + "-"
print(result)

sk1.title: Keep a running value across iterations
sk1.bodyMarkdown:
A loop can remember work from earlier repetitions by storing a value **before** the loop and updating it **inside** the loop.

Two common patterns are:

- a **counter**: how many matching events have happened;
- an **accumulator**: a running result such as a numeric total.

Example accumulator:

```python
numbers = [3, 5, 2]
total = 0

for n in numbers:
    total = total + n

print(total)
```

The running values of `total` are:

```text
0 -> 3 -> 8 -> 10
```

The important pattern is:

1. initialize the stored result before the loop;
2. read its current value inside the loop;
3. combine that value with the current item;
4. store the new result back in the same variable.

`total += n` is a shorter way to write `total = total + n`.

sk2.title: Increase a counter only when something matches
sk2.bodyMarkdown:
A counter normally starts at `0` because nothing has matched yet.

```python
word = "banana"
vowel_count = 0

for ch in word:
    if ch in "aeiou":
        vowel_count = vowel_count + 1

print(vowel_count)
```

The loop visits every character, but the counter changes only when the condition is true.

For `"banana"`:

```text
b -> count stays 0
a -> count becomes 1
n -> count stays 1
a -> count becomes 2
n -> count stays 2
a -> count becomes 3
```

The final output is `3`.

This is a **conditional counter**: initialize once, test each item, and increment only for matches.

sk3.title: Accumulate only the values you want
sk3.bodyMarkdown:
An accumulator can also update only when an item passes a condition.

```python
numbers = [4, 7, 2, 9, 6]
even_total = 0

for n in numbers:
    if n % 2 == 0:
        even_total = even_total + n

print(even_total)
```

Only the even values are added:

```text
start: 0
add 4 -> 4
skip 7
add 2 -> 6
skip 9
add 6 -> 12
```

The final output is `12`.

The difference from a counter is the update:

- counter: usually add `1`;
- numeric accumulator: add the current value or another calculated amount.

A running result can also be text, but the same rule still applies: initialize before the loop and update the stored result during the loop.
